title: Pattern guide
text:
Piece
Meaning in today’s examples
Example




John
Literal characters
John 8:31


\d
A digit
Chapter or verse number


\s
Whitespace, including the nonbreaking space in this dataset
1 Nephi


[.-]
One listed character
A dot or hyphen


\.
A literal dot
The dot in an email domain


{5}
Exactly five repetitions
A five digit ZIP code


{1,3}
Between one and three repetitions
Chapter digits


+
One or more repetitions
\d+


?
Zero or one of the previous item
An optional verse range


(?:A|B)
Either A or B, without capturing a field
Two book names


(?P<book>...)
Capture and name a field
The book column


\b
Boundary between word and nonword characters
Before a ZIP code


^ and $
Start and end of a line/string in the usual single-line case
Checking a whole field
In Python, write regex strings as raw strings, such as r"\d{5}", so Python passes the backslashes to the regex engine. re.search() finds text inside a larger string. re.fullmatch() checks an entire string. re.findall() returns the matches, and pandas .str.extractall() makes a row for each captured match.

title: Pattern guide
text:
Things to test

Does the pattern match inside a longer value when it should not?
Does punctuation change the result?
Does the input contain a nonbreaking space or an en dash?
Are there two matches in one string, and are both returned?
Does the pattern capture only the intended book, chapter, and verses?

The citation pattern in this lesson describes recognizable text. It does not verify that a chapter or verse exists. The email example similarly finds common shapes without covering every valid address.

title: Regular expressions
text: We begin with a review of cleaning pipelines and learn to describe families of strings when values vary in predictable ways. The same slide deck continues with group challenges on optional and alternative forms, then builds a scripture citation pattern in stages and tests it against actual conference talks.

title: Regular expressions
text:
Today’s question
How can a short pattern describe ZIP codes, phone numbers, email addresses, or a simple scripture reference? How can we tell when it matches too much or misses something?

title: Regular expressions
text:
Materials

Lecture slides, with prediction questions and their answers.
Pattern guide for looking up the syntax used in class.

title: Regular expressions
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do

Explain how literal characters, classes, groups, and quantifiers combine into a pattern.
Distinguish finding text inside a string from checking an entire field.
Read a short regex, predict its matches, and explain a counterexample.
Write and defend a short pattern with your group at the whiteboard.
Decide when a whole piece is optional and when forms require alternatives.
Recognize a plausible partial match and test a composed citation rule against the talk sample.

The talk examples are a small introduction to extraction. The lab will carry the fuller workflow. The earlier combined lecture and notebooks remain in the source package as drafts.

Review: when a pipeline meets a new value
Last week, our book-name column contained Matt. and Matthew. We standardized Matt. to Matthew.
A new batch contains Matt too.
Talk with a neighbor: What would you change? What must you keep if some rows were already processed under the earlier rule?

Matt.

An exact replacement works here because we have a small set of known values in a book-name field. We should not replace every occurrence of Matt in a whole talk.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Today’s problem
What if the number and placement of characters vary?
84043              84043-4820
801-555-0142       801.555.0142
tom@byu.edu        tom7@byu.edu
John 8:31          Alma 34:32
We need a way to describe the strings we want to find, rather than list them one at a time.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: A regex describes a set of strings
text:
A regex describes a set of strings
Alma 7:12 is one value. The pattern Alma \d+:\d+ describes many:
Alma 7:12     ✓
Alma 34:32    ✓
John 8:31     ✗
The book and punctuation stay fixed. The chapter and verse can change. Here \d stands for a digit, and + means one or more of the preceding item. We will work through those pieces before asking you to build a pattern.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
How we build larger patterns
A regex is made from a few types of instructions:



Instruction
What it lets us describe




Exact text
A fixed book name or punctuation mark


A choice
One allowed character or one allowed word


Repetition
A chapter with one, two, or more digits


Position
The beginning of a field or a word boundary



Putting instructions next to each other describes their order. We will learn the notation for each one in the next few examples.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: Searching and checking a whole field
text:
Searching and checking a whole field
re.search() finds a pattern inside a string. re.fullmatch() checks whether the entire string fits.
Our pattern is the literal text "cat". We wrap each result in bool() so the answer is True if there is a match and False otherwise. What will these three checks return?
import re

bool(re.search("cat", "The cat slept"))
bool(re.fullmatch("cat", "The cat slept"))
bool(re.fullmatch("cat", "cat"))
Predict with a neighbor, then compare with the next slide.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Check: search versus fullmatch
search("cat", "The cat slept")     → True
fullmatch("cat", "The cat slept")  → False
fullmatch("cat", "cat")            → True
We used bool() to ask whether a match exists. A search can succeed even when the whole field does not fit the rule.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Literal characters and the dot
Most characters match themselves. Some have special meanings.
r"byu.edu": the dot matches almost any character.
r"byu\.edu": the escaped dot matches a literal period.
The r tells Python to pass the backslash to the regex engine. We will write patterns as raw strings from here on.
With a neighbor: Which pattern accepts byuXedu? Which accepts byu.edu?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Check the dot
values = ["byu.edu", "byuXedu"]
for pattern in [r"byu.edu", r"byu\.edu"]:
    print(pattern, [bool(re.fullmatch(pattern, v)) for v in values])
byu.edu   [True, True]
byu\.edu  [True, False]
Escaping changes a special character back into the literal character.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Character classes choose one character
[.-] matches one dot or hyphen. A range such as [A-Z] matches one capital letter.
We can combine ranges: [A-Za-z0-9] matches one letter or digit. We will use that in the email exercise.
r"801[-.]555"   matches   801-555   and   801.555
Inside [ ], a dot usually has its ordinary meaning. Outside, . is a wildcard.
Predict: Would [.-] match the two-character string .- as a whole field?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
A negative character class
[^aeiou] means one character other than a lowercase vowel.
[bool(re.fullmatch(r"[^aeiou]", x)) for x in ["a", "b", "7"]]
[False, True, True]
It also accepts 7. “Not a vowel” is broader than “a consonant.”

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Useful shorthand classes



Pattern
One matching character




\d
digit


\s
whitespace, including many spaces that look ordinary


\w
word character, including letters, digits, and _


\D, \S, \W
the corresponding opposites



\w is convenient, but it may include characters your task did not intend. In Python, it can also include Unicode letters.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Quantifiers change how many



Pattern
Number of repetitions
Example




\d{3}
exactly 3
801


\d{2,4}
2 to 4
12, 8421


\d+
at least 1
7, 343


\d*
0 or more
"", 77


u?
0 or 1
color, colour in colou?r



A quantifier acts on the item immediately before it. That item can be a character or a class. On the next slides, we will make a whole group count as one item.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Groups choose whole alternatives
(?:red|blue) car allows red car or blue car.
[(v, bool(re.fullmatch(r"(?:red|blue) car", v)))
 for v in ["red car", "blue car", "red truck"]]
[('red car', True), ('blue car', True), ('red truck', False)]
(?: ... ) groups a choice. | separates the alternatives. We will use a named capturing group tomorrow when we need an extracted column.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: A class and a group are different
text:
A class and a group are different



Pattern
Its choice




[cd]
one character, c or d


(?:cat|dog)
one word, cat or dog



Predict: Does [cat|dog] match the whole word cat? Why might it still find something inside cat with re.search?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: Check the class and the group
text:
Check the class and the group
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"[cat|dog]", "cat")))
print(re.search(r"[cat|dog]", "cat").group())
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"(?:cat|dog)", "cat")))
False
'c'
True
[cat|dog] still consumes one character. For whole words, choose between groups of characters.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Pause: what is being repeated?
Compare these patterns on the whole string hahaha!:
r"ha+!"       # repeat the a
r"(?:ha)+!"   # repeat the group ha
Think, then pair: Which one matches? What string might the other match instead?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Check the quantifier’s scope
[(p, bool(re.fullmatch(p, "hahaha!")))
 for p in [r"ha+!", r"(?:ha)+!"]]
[('ha+!', False), ('(?:ha)+!', True)]
ha+! accepts haaa!. (?:ha)+! accepts hahaha!.
The parentheses determine what the + repeats.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Positions are different from characters



Position
Meaning in today’s examples




^
start of the string


$
end of the string


\b
boundary between a word and a nonword character



These symbols do not consume a character. A word boundary can occur next to punctuation, not only next to a space.
For a whole field, re.fullmatch() often states our question more directly than adding ^ and $.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Read and decipher
First think alone, then compare with a partner. Put each pattern into words. Give an example it accepts and one it rejects.

r"\bcat\b"
r"\b\d{5}\b"
r"^[A-Z][a-z]+$"

For #2, what would re.search return from 84043-4820?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: Read and decipher: discuss the answers
text:
Read and decipher: discuss the answers








Pattern
Reads as
Example match




\bcat\b
the word cat
cat!, but not bobcat


\b\d{5}\b
a five-digit token
84043 in 84043-4820


^[A-Z][a-z]+$
a capitalized word with more lowercase letters
Kerby, but not KERBY



Which result might be misleading? A match to the first five digits does not establish that the entire field is a plain five-digit ZIP.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Whiteboard challenge
Divide into four groups. If there are more than four groups, repeat A through D.

Write a short regex without Python quotes for your group’s whole-field rule.
Check both accepted examples and the rejected example mentally.
Write the pattern on the board. Explain each piece and propose a new test that could challenge it.

5 minutes to work, 7 minutes to share. Wait for each explanation before viewing the solution slides.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Pick up yesterday’s board work
Your four groups wrote working rules for ZIP codes, phone numbers, campus emails, and John/Alma citations. Today every group will solve each new case.
Start with the ZIP rule from the board: \d{5}(?:-\d{4})?
In your group: Which whole piece does ? make optional? Why would \d{5}-?\d{4} describe a different set of strings?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Optional means the whole group



Pattern
Accepts
Also accepts




\d{5}(?:-\d{4})?
84043
84043-4820


\d{5}-?\d{4}
840434820
84043-4820



The parentheses make the hyphen and four digits one optional piece. ? applies to the item immediately before it.
To match a literal parenthesis in a phone number, write \( or \); bare parentheses group a regex.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Group challenge 1: phone numbers
Our board rule handled 801-555-0142 and 801.555.0142. Extend it to handle parentheses too.



Accept as whole fields
Reject




801-555-0142
(801 555 0142


801.555.0142
8015550142


(801) 555 0142




All groups: Write a rule; explain how it treats the area code and the separator after it. Use \( and \) for literal parentheses. 3 minutes, then compare approaches.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: One phone rule and its limits
text:
One phone rule and its limits
import re

phone = r"(?:\d{3}[-.]|\(\d{3}\) )\d{3}[-. ]\d{4}"
values = ["801-555-0142", "801.555.0142", "(801) 555 0142",
          "(801 555 0142", "8015550142"]
for value in values:
    print(value, bool(re.fullmatch(phone, value)))
801-555-0142 True
801.555.0142 True
(801) 555 0142 True
(801 555 0142 False
8015550142 False
New test: It also accepts 801-555.0142. Would that matter for your data?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: A choice is different from an option
text:
A choice is different from an option
For an email written two ways, we need a separator in each position. We choose which form it takes:



Choice
Matches




(?:@| \(at\) )
@ or (at)


(?:\.| \(dot\) )
. or (dot)



There is no ? here: omitting the separator would make an invalid address. The spaces around (at) and (dot) are part of those choices.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Group challenge 2: written-out emails



Accept as whole fields
Reject




tom@byu.com
tom@byuXcom


tom (at) byu (dot) com
tom at byu dot com


amy7@gmail.com




All groups: Compose a rule from the two choices on the previous slide. For this exercise, the username has letters or digits, the provider has letters, and the ending is com.
3 minutes: Test both ordinary and written-out forms. Does your pattern also accept a mixed form?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: One email rule and a decision
text:
One email rule and a decision
email = (r"[A-Za-z0-9]+(?:@| \(at\) )[A-Za-z]+"
         r"(?:\.| \(dot\) )com")
values = ["tom@byu.com", "tom (at) byu (dot) com",
          "amy7@gmail.com", "tom@byuXcom", "tom at byu dot com"]
for value in values:
    print(value, bool(re.fullmatch(email, value)))
tom@byu.com True
tom (at) byu (dot) com True
amy7@gmail.com True
tom@byuXcom False
tom at byu dot com False
This rule also accepts tom@byu (dot) com. If that mixture is not meaningful, we could check for it or standardize the written-out form in a data pipeline first.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Group challenge 3: verse ranges
Yesterday’s John/Alma board rule was (?:John|Alma) \d+:\d+. Keep single verses and allow ranges too.



Accept as whole fields
Reject




John 8:31
John 8:31–


John 8:31-32
Mosiah 3:19


Alma 34:32–33




All groups: Which whole piece should be optional? A range can use a hyphen or an en dash. 3 minutes, then defend your pattern.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: One rule for one verse or a range
text:
One rule for one verse or a range
short_citation = r"(?:John|Alma)\s+\d+:\d+(?:[-–]\d+)?"
values = ["John 8:31", "John 8:31-32", "Alma 34:32–33",
          "John 8:31–", "Mosiah 3:19"]
for value in values:
    print(value, bool(re.fullmatch(short_citation, value)))
John 8:31 True
John 8:31-32 True
Alma 34:32–33 True
John 8:31– False
Mosiah 3:19 False
(?:[-–]\d+)? makes the dash and ending verse digits optional together. \s+ accepts a space between book and chapter.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Finding text changes the question
re.fullmatch checks one entire field. re.findall returns the exact substrings found inside longer text.
text = "John 8:31–32; Alma 34:32–33"
old_rule = r"(?:John|Alma) \d+:\d+"
print(re.findall(old_rule, text))
print(re.findall(short_citation, text))
['John 8:31', 'Alma 34:32']
['John 8:31–32', 'Alma 34:32–33']
Tell a partner: Why were the old matches plausible but incomplete? A good match test checks the entire returned substring.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: Build together: which book forms matter?
text:
Build together: which book forms matter?
Our two talks contain 1 Nephi, Nephi, John, Alma, Mosiah, D&C, and Doctrine and Covenants. We may also encounter Matt. and Matthew in other text.
As a class: Start with the John/Alma rule. What change to the book part would cover each new form? Which parts of the chapter and verse rule can stay the same?
Our board rule deliberately rejected Mosiah 3:19. For extraction from these talks, that example should now match. We are extending our tested set of book forms, not claiming to recognize every possible scripture citation.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Add the numbered book
book = r"(?:John|Alma|Mosiah|(?:1\s+)?Nephi)"
(?:1\s+)?Nephi handles 1 Nephi and Nephi. The \s+ also handles the nonbreaking space in 1 Nephi from our talk text.
Before moving on: Why would 1?\s+Nephi fail to express this choice? What would you test to see whether matching only Nephi ever hides a longer book name?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Add names and abbreviations
book = (
    r"(?:John|Alma|Mosiah|(?:1\s+)?Nephi|"
    r"D&C|Doctrine and Covenants|"
    r"Matt(?:hew|\.))"
)
D&C and Doctrine and Covenants are two complete alternatives. Matt(?:hew|\.) shares the Matt prefix, then chooses hew or a literal period.
Check together: Which branch accepts Matt. 5:3? Which accepts Matthew 5:3? Which book did we add after yesterday’s group challenge?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Compose the pieces and predict
chapter_verse = r"\d+:\d+(?:[-–]\d+)?"
citation = r"\b" + book + r"\s+" + chapter_verse + r"\b"
text = "Matt. 5:3; Matthew 5:3; 1 Nephi 8:27; D&C 19:16"
print(re.findall(citation, text))
First predict with a neighbor: Which exact four substrings should appear? \b marks a word boundary so a book name cannot start in the middle of another word, or a verse end in the middle of a word.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Check the composed rule
['Matt. 5:3', 'Matthew 5:3', '1 Nephi 8:27', 'D&C 19:16']
The pattern is built from three parts: book choice, space, and chapter:verse with an optional range. Our constructed test checks those parts together before we use real talks.
New test: If someone wrote 2 Nephi 9:14, would our rule return the entire reference? Predict before we try it.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Check real talk text
import pandas as pd

talks = pd.read_csv("data/talks_sample.csv")
for name, talk_text in zip(talks["talk_name"], talks["text"]):
    matches = re.findall(citation, talk_text)
    print(f"{name}: {len(matches)} matches")
Now Is the Time: 7 matches
The Sacrament Can Help Us Become Holy: 6 matches
These are counts for the book forms we included. Before calling them scripture totals, we would inspect the returned strings and look for missed or partial citations.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: A test that challenges our rule
text:
A test that challenges our rule
print(re.findall(citation, "2 Nephi 9:14; John 8:31–"))
['Nephi 9:14', 'John 8:31']
Neither substring is the complete reference we intended to extract. \b does not prevent a match beginning after 2 or ending before a dash.
In pairs: Name one change or test you would try next. Decide whether to expand the book choices, inspect context around matches, or standardize the source text first.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Exit question
Choose one of today’s three group problems. Which piece of its rule is optional, and which piece is an either-or choice?
For citations, give one case our current rule handles and one it mishandles. What test would reveal the difference?
In lab, we can extend the book forms, inspect both missed and accidental matches, and build a reusable extraction pipeline.
